M9 · Exam-style induction machine problems (Ch7)

Why this matters in the exam: Q3 (20 marks) is “AC and Induction Machines” every year. Its last part is always a full equivalent-circuit calculation: Jun23 Q3c (9 marks, torque at rated speed plus input current, and motor or generator) and Jun24 Q3c (10 marks, generator at 1025 rpm: slip, , , , , ). Add the test-parameter part (Jun24 Q3b, 4 marks) and the max-torque part (Jun23 Q3b, 5 marks) from M8, and about 14 of the 20 Q3 marks are this one circuit. Ch7 has no worked exam solutions in the files, only numerical answers, so this pack gives full exam layouts checked against those answers.

M7 covered the fundamentals. M8 covered the tests, maximum torque and generator mode. This pack is about speed: solving a full question cleanly in about 30 minutes.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The circuit the course uses (Lecture 7.4.4, 7.6.1)

2. The method

2.1 Timed strategy for a 20-mark Q3

The exam is 120 minutes for 80 marks, which is 1.5 minutes per mark. Q3 gets 30 minutes. Do not let it run over: Q4 (Ch8) has the same structure.

Part (past pattern) Marks Time What to write
Q3a: machine basics (poles, , ideal efficiency, linear τ–n, or curve sketches) 6 8 min One line per answer. for ideal efficiency. See M6.
Q3b: tests (Jun24) or max torque (Jun23) 4–5 7 min Use the M8 playbooks.
Q3c: full equivalent-circuit calculation 9–10 14 min The layout in 2.2 below.
Check signs, units and “per phase vs total” – 1 min

Rules that save time:

  1. Write the “header block” first for Q3c, before reading the parts in detail: , , , , , . Two or three marks are always in it (Jun23 c(i), Jun24 c(i)), and every later part needs it.
  2. Write the series impedance once in both forms, e.g. . Then the current is one division.
  3. Keep 4 significant figures in the calculator. Round only the boxed answer.
  4. If you get stuck on a part, carry on. Each Q3c part is independently markable. If you cannot get , still do from the torque formula.
  5. Draw the circuit if asked (Jun24 c(ii)). Label every element with its value as an impedance (e.g. , ). This is 1 easy mark.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Line voltage in a per-phase circuit. For star, V. For delta, , and the line current is .
  • Dividing by instead of for torque. . Then . Mixing these up gives an error of about (3–5 %), which loses the mark.
  • Using instead of in , or using for rotor copper loss. Rotor copper loss is (Lecture 7.5.1, “not divided by slip”).
  • Slip at the wrong speed. The rated speed fixes the pole count. The slip is calculated at the operating speed (1520 rpm in Jun23 c(ii), 1025 rpm in Jun24 c(i)).
  • Dropping the minus sign in generator mode. , , , and are all negative. The course answers keep the signs (, , W, Nm).
  • Adding currents in polar form. must be done in rectangular form.
  • Including when told to ignore it (or the reverse). Read each part. In 7.14(a) you ignore it. In 7.14(b) you must not (the course hint says 93.7 A means you forgot it).
  • Rounding early. instead of 6.000 is harmless, but rounded to 0.1 is not. Keep as an exact fraction.

(d) The rotor has no separate excitation. The rotating flux is set up only by the stator magnetising current through , which comes from the supply. So the machine always draws lagging reactive power ( per phase, plus the leakage VArs), whether motoring or generating. The grid (or local capacitors) must provide these VArs. A stand-alone induction generator needs a capacitor bank. [3]

 P_AG = 3 I2'^2 R2'/s     τ = P_AG / ws     P_OUT = τ w = (1-s) P_AG
